paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who we left hammering on the heavy locked gates of the widow Morozov’s house, did get himself heard in the end. Fenya was still shaken by the scare she had had two hours before, and was too “upset” to go to bed. The furious pounding at the gate almost threw her into hysterics. She had watched him drive away with her own eyes, yet she imagined it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again, because nobody else could knock so savagely. She ran to the house-porter, who had already woken and gone out to the gate, and begged him not to open it. But the porter questioned Pyotr Ilyitch and found out that he wanted to see Fenya about very “important business,” and finally he decided to open up. Pyotr Ilyitch was shown into Fenya’s kitchen, though the girl asked him to let the house-porter stay with them, “because of her misgivings.” He started questioning her, and right away he got the most vital fact. When Dmitri Fyodorovitch ran out to look for Grushenka, he had grabbed a pestle from the mortar. When he came back he no longer had it, and his hands were smeared with blood.

“And the blood was simply pouring off him, dripping, dripping!” Fenya kept crying. That gruesome detail was only her overheated imagination at work. But even if the blood was not “dripping,” Pyotr Ilyitch had seen those bloody hands himself, and had helped wash them. Besides, what he had to settle was not how fast the blood dried. He had to settle where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run with the pestle, or rather, whether it really was to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, and how he could be sure of it. Pyotr Ilyitch kept pressing this point. He found out nothing conclusive, but he left convinced that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere except his father’s house, and so something must have happened there.

“And when he came back,” Fenya went on eagerly, “I told him the whole story, and then I started asking him, ‘Why have you got blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?’ And he said it was human blood, and that he’d just killed someone. He admitted it all to me, and suddenly he ran off like a madman. I sat down and began thinking, where’s he running off to now, like a madman? He’ll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. So I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running to his lodgings, but I looked toward Plotnikov’s shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya had noticed this and remembered it.) Fenya’s old grandmother backed up her story as best she could. Pyotr Ilyitch asked a few more questions and left the house more upset and uneasy than he had been when he came in.

The easiest and most obvious thing would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s and find out whether anything had happened there and, if so, what. Only once he was sure of that would he go to the police captain, which Pyotr Ilyitch firmly meant to do. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s gates were stout, and he would have to knock all over again. He barely knew Fyodor Pavlovitch. And what if they let him in after all that knocking and nothing had happened? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, with his sneering way, would tell the story around town of how a stranger called Perhotin had burst in on him at midnight to ask if anyone had killed him. It would be a scandal. And Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded scandal more than anything in the world.

Still, the feeling that had hold of him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and cursed himself, he set off again, not to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s but to Madame Hohlakov’s. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he would go straight to the police captain. If she said she had given him the money, he would go home and leave the matter until morning.

It is obvious, of course, that turning up at eleven at night at the house of a fashionable lady he had never met, perhaps dragging her out of bed to put an astonishing question to her, was an even better way to cause a scandal than going to Fyodor Pavlovitch. But that is how it goes at times, especially in cases like this one, with the decisions of the most exact and level-headed people. And at that moment Pyotr Ilyitch was anything but level-headed. For the rest of his life he remembered how a nagging uneasiness crept over him, growing more and more painful and pushing him on against his will. The whole way he kept cursing himself, naturally, for going to this lady. But “I’ll get to the bottom of it, I will!” he told himself for the tenth time, gritting his teeth, and he did what he had set out to do.

It was exactly eleven when he walked into Madame Hohlakov’s house. They let him into the yard fairly quickly, but when he asked if the lady was still up, the porter could say only that she usually went to bed by that hour.
“Ask at the top of the stairs. If the lady wants to see you, she’ll see you. If she doesn’t, she won’t.”

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but it was not so easy here. The footman did not want to announce him, and at last he called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch asked her politely but stubbornly to tell her mistress that an official who lived in the town, named Perhotin, had come on particular business, and that he would never have dared come if it were not of the greatest importance. “Tell her in those words, in just those words,” he told the girl.

She went off. He stayed waiting in the entry. Madame Hohlakov was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She had felt upset ever since Mitya’s visit, and she had a feeling she would not get through the night without the sick headache that always came over her after such excitement. She was surprised by the maid’s report. She irritably refused to see him. All the same, the unexpected call at such an hour from an “official living in the town,” a complete stranger, aroused her feminine curiosity enormously. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch dug his heels in like a mule. He earnestly begged the maid to go back with another message, in these exact words:
“That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might regret it later if she refused to see him now.”
“I jumped in headfirst,” he said afterward, describing it.

The maid gave him an astonished look and went to take his message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought it over for a moment, asked what he looked like, and was told he was “very well dressed, young and so polite.” I should mention, by the way, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and knew it. Madame Hohlakov made up her mind to see him. She was in her dressing-gown and slippers, but she threw a black shawl over her shoulders. “The official” was shown into the drawing-room, the same room where Mitya had been received a little earlier. The lady came to meet her visitor with a stern, questioning face, and without asking him to sit down she began at once with the question:
“What do you want?”
“I’ve taken the liberty of troubling you, madam, about our mutual acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.
But he had barely spoken the name when the lady’s face showed sharp irritation. She nearly screamed, and broke in on him furiously:

“How much longer am I going to be plagued by that dreadful man?” she cried hysterically. “How dare you, sir, how could you presume to disturb a lady you don’t know, in her own house at such an hour!... And to force yourself on her to talk about a man who came here, into this very drawing-room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and went stamping out of the room, the way no one leaves a decent house. I’ll have you know, sir, that I shall file a complaint against you, and I will not let this pass. Kindly leave at once.... I am a mother.... I ... I—”
“Murder! So he tried to murder you, too?”
“Why, has he killed somebody else?” Madame Hohlakov asked impulsively.

“If you’ll listen for half a moment, madam, I’ll explain it all in a couple of words,” Perhotin answered firmly. “At five o’clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact that he had no money. Yet at nine o’clock he came to my place with a wad of hundred-rouble notes in his hand, two or three thousand roubles’ worth. His hands and face were smeared with blood, and he looked like a madman. I asked him where he’d got so much money, and he said he had just got it from you, that you had given him three thousand to go off to the gold-mines....”
Madame Hohlakov’s face took on a look of intense, painful excitement.
“Good God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, wringing her hands. “I never gave him any money, never! Oh, run, run!... Not another word! Save the old man ... run to his father ... run!”
“Pardon me, madam, so you did not give him money? You remember for certain that you gave him no money at all?”

“No, I didn’t, I didn’t! I refused him, because he wouldn’t have known how to value it. He ran out in a fury, stamping. He flew at me, but I slipped away.... And let me tell you, since I want to hide nothing from you now, that he actually spat at me. Can you imagine! But why are we standing? Ah, sit down.”
“Pardon me, I....”
“Or better still, run, run, you must run and save the poor old man from a terrible death!”
“But what if he’s already killed him?”
“Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do? What do you think we should do now?”

By now she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down, and she sat facing him. Briefly, but quite clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her what had happened, or at least the part he had seen himself. He told her about his visit to Fenya, too, and about the pestle. All these details overwhelmed the distracted lady. She kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands....

“Would you believe it, I saw all this coming! I have that special gift, whatever I picture comes true. And how many times I’ve looked at that dreadful man and thought, that man will end up murdering me. And now it’s happened ... that is, if he hasn’t murdered me but only his own father, it’s only because the finger of God kept me safe. And besides, he was ashamed to murder me because, right here, I put the holy ikon from the relics of the holy martyr Saint Varvara around his neck.... And to think how close I was to death at that moment, I went right up to him and he stretched out his neck to me!... Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch (I think you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch), I don’t believe in miracles, but that ikon and this unmistakable miracle with me now—it shakes me, and I’m ready to believe anything you like. Have you heard about Father Zossima?... But I don’t know what I’m saying ... and just think, with the ikon on his neck he spat at me.... He only spat, it’s true, he didn’t murder me and ... off he dashed! But what shall we do, what must we do now? What do you think?”
Pyotr Ilyitch stood up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain to tell him all about it, and would leave it to the captain to do whatever he saw fit.

“Oh, he’s an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he’s just the person to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you’ve thought of everything! I’d never have thought of it, in your place!”

“Particularly since I know the police captain quite well myself,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. He was still on his feet, and plainly wanted to get away as fast as he could from this impulsive lady, who would not let him say goodbye and go.

“And be sure, be sure,” she chattered on, “to come back and tell me what you see there, and what you find out ... what comes to light ... how they’ll try him ... and what they sentence him to.... Tell me, we have no death penalty, do we? But be sure to come, even if it’s three in the morning, or four, or half-past four.... Tell them to wake me, to wake me, to shake me if I don’t get up.... But, good heavens, I won’t be able to sleep! Oh, but wait, shouldn’t I come with you?”
“N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, saying that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, it might perhaps be of some use ... in case it’s needed....”

“Of course!” Madame Hohlakov skipped over to her bureau, delighted. “And you know, I’m simply struck, amazed at how resourceful you are, how sensible in these matters. Are you in the service here? I’m so pleased to think you’re in the service here!”
And, still talking, she scribbled these lines on half a sheet of notepaper:

I’ve never in my life lent three thousand roubles today to that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, in spite of everything, he is unhappy). I’ve never given him money, never: That I swear by all that’s holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
“Here’s the note!” she said, turning quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go, save him. It’s a noble thing you’re doing!”
And she crossed him three times. She ran out to walk him to the passage.

“How grateful I am to you! You can’t imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it that I’ve never met you before? I shall feel flattered to see you at my house from now on. How delightful that you live here!... Such precision! Such practical ability!... They must value you, they must understand you. If there’s anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people! I’m in love with young people! The younger generation is the one support of our suffering country. Her one hope.... Oh, go, go!...”

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already run off, or she would not have let him go so soon. Still, Madame Hohlakov had made a rather pleasant impression on him, and it had softened somewhat his worry at being drawn into so unpleasant an affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. “She’s not so old at all,” he thought, pleased with himself. “Why, I would have taken her for her own daughter.”

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply charmed with the young man. “Such sense! Such exactness! In so young a man! In our day! And all with such manners and looks! They say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here’s the proof!” and so on. So she simply forgot the “dreadful affair,” and only when she was getting into bed, as she suddenly remembered “how near death she had been,” did she exclaim: “Ah, it is awful, awful!”
But she fell at once into a deep, sweet sleep.

I would not have lingered over such trifling and irrelevant details, though, if this odd meeting between the young official and the by no means elderly widow had not turned out afterward to be the foundation of that practical and precise young man’s whole career. His story is still remembered with amazement in our town, and perhaps I shall have something to say about it once I have finished my long history of the Brothers Karamazov.
